This is NPR News Now. The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Dale Willman. People on the Gulf Coast are being urged to take shelter
as Hurricane Isaias moves inland. It's the first hurricane of what has been an unusually quiet
Atlantic season. Emperor Sergio Martinez Beltran is in Pensacola, Florida.
Widespread power outages are also expected along with tornadoes and flash flooding as the storm
moves inland Saturday. Rainfall totals over the weekend could reach up to 15 inches in parts of
Alabama, Florida and Georgia. Isaias is the first hurricane of the Atlantic season and the first
hurricane since 2024 to hit the U.S. That's NPR's Sergio Martinez Beltran. With our report,
more than 600,000 homes are now without power in Florida and Alabama.
Vice President J.D. Vance is casting doubt on whether the execution of the man who shot
and killed more than a dozen people at Fort Hood in 2009 will be live streamed. The Pentagon said
earlier this week his execution by firing squad would be made publicly available.
Emperor Deepa Shivram has our reports. Vance is campaigning in Ohio and told reporters he
didn't know if the live stream would actually happen and he added that if the execution is
live streamed he wouldn't watch it. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth's decision to live stream
the execution received widespread condemnation from lawmakers in the U.S. from both parties
and from international bodies like the United Nations. The shooter in Adal Hassan killed 13
people and wounded more than 30 in Fort Hood, Texas. His execution is scheduled for December 3rd,
17 years to the day since the shooting took place. Deepa Shivram, NPR News, the White House.
Hours after an international humanitarian legal expert was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize,
the State Department announced sanctions on the International Criminal Court.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio has vowed to dismantle the world's only standing war crimes
tribunal as NPR's Michelle Kellerman reports. Secretary Rubio says the U.S. will ban transactions
with what he calls a rogue court, cutting off its resources and crippling its ability to operate.
America never joined the court. We don't need that court and we don't want it.
The ICC was set up as a court of last resort for victims of war crimes, crimes against humanity,
and genocide. The U.S. protested an investigation into Afghanistan which could have implicated U.S.
service members. The ICC closed that investigation. The U.S. also opposes the arrest warrant against
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over the war in Gaza. The ICC says in a statement that
it will not be deterred but its fate now rests in the hands of the states that created it.
Michelle Kellerman, NPR News, Washington. Stocks closed up on Wall Street Friday. The
Dow Jones Industrial Average was up by 423 points. The NASDAQ closed up 172 points while the S&P
500 closed up 46 points. You're listening to NPR News.
President Trump says he has a deal with Russia to get diesel fuel. Trump posted on social media
Friday that he made the deal during a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
It's being seen as an effort to deal with high fuel prices just before the midterm elections
next month. The move is a reversal of years of U.S. pressure on Moscow over its war with Ukraine.
Ukraine's president is calling the decision a weak decision by strong partners.
The Kennedy Center is named a talent manager for 1980s and 1990s rock acts as its new executive
director. NPR's Anastasia Zilukas has more. Rick Kenney has worked with acts including ZZ Top,
former Motley crew drummer Tommy Lee, and Creed frontman Scott Stapp. He's worked as a consultant
for the Kennedy Center since shortly after President Trump became the arts institutions
chairman in February 2025. Kenney's appointment seems to be part of the center's current push
away from the kind of orchestras, ballet groups, theater troupes, and marquee contemporary artists
more typically booked by the Kennedy Center and similar premier arts venues around the country.
The Kennedy Center declined to comment on Kenney's appointment.
Anastasia Zilukas, NPR News, New York. Police in Italy say thieves have stolen
about 30,000 bottles of premium wine worth about five million euros. The producer says it's the
biggest wine theft in Italian history. The thieves targeted a facility near Cortona and used the
producer's equipment to load the bottles onto two trucks. The theft occurred last weekend,
but the producer made the news public on Friday. I'm Dale Willman, NPR News.
